why: Any 2p books can be bought with p pair purchases (buy the outside ones singly, then pair the outermost chosen books inward), so the order constraint disappears: pair up the most expensive books while each pair costs more than pairCost. It is scheduled in the DP week, but sorting plus a greedy prefix replaces the interval DP.
hints: The left/right rule looks like an interval DP. Before writing one, ask: which sets of books can be covered by p pair purchases?
Any set of 2p books can be: remove the books outside the chosen set one by one, pair the outermost two chosen books, and repeat inward. So pair purchases should go to the 2p most expensive books.
Sort costs descending; for p = 1..k the saving is (sum of the 2p largest) - p * pairCost; take the best saving (0 if none helps) and subtract it from the total. O(n log n).
pitfalls: Using a pair purchase is not always good: in [1, 1, 1] with pairCost 2, no pair helps.
With an odd number of books left, the last one must be bought singly (the pair needs two different books).
k caps the number of pair uses; you do not have to use all of them, and p can be at most n // 2.
Totals reach about 10^14; keep them in 64-bit.
constraints:
• 1 <= n <= 10^5 (the source's bound is garbled; this is a reasonable reading)
  • 1 <= cost[i] <= 10^9
  • 1 <= pairCost <= 10^9
  • 1 <= k <= n
  • cost is not necessarily sorted
